subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
passage: Monday. Urmila, two, jammed the star block at the round hole again and again, then threw it and wailed. Wednesday. Her papa, Darshan, sat beside her and turned the star a little in her fingers, just enough. She pushed. Clunk! It dropped in. Urmila clapped and shouted, "Me did it!" Saturday. She picked up the star, turned it herself, wiggled it, and it fell through. She looked at Papa, beaming, then fed the box the moon block too.

qa.q: Which block did Urmila jam at the round hole?
qa.a: The star block.

qa.q: What does Urmila's shout 'Me did it!' suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt proud, as if the win were entirely her own, even though Darshan had turned the star for her.

qa.q: Why was turning the star just a little a good choice for Darshan?
qa.a: It gave just enough help for Urmila to push it in herself, so she kept trying and later managed alone.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel on Saturday, watching Urmila turn the star by herself?
qa.a: Darshan is likely delighted, seeing his small help on Wednesday grow into something she can do alone.

grounding: A toddler fails to fit a block alone, succeeds when her father turns it slightly, beams as if it were all her own win, and later manages by herself.

subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
passage: In the front room of their Pune flat, Shreya, two and a half, put the fourth block on her tower. It swayed and crashed. She stamped her foot. Nazia Khala knelt and rested one finger lightly against the side of the new tower. "Try again, jaan." Shreya placed block four, then five, tongue poking out. The tower wobbled but held. Shreya squealed and ran to the kitchen door. "Look! I made it big!" Khala quietly took her finger away.

qa.q: What happened when Shreya first put the fourth block on her tower?
qa.a: It swayed and crashed.

qa.q: Why did Shreya run to the kitchen door shouting?
qa.a: She was proud and excited, believing she had made the tall tower all by herself.

qa.q: What choice did Nazia Khala make that helped, and why?
qa.a: She rested one finger against the tower instead of building it for Shreya, so Shreya still placed every block.

qa.q: Why might Khala have taken her finger away quietly?
qa.a: Khala wanted Shreya to keep the joy of the win as her own, without being reminded of the help.

grounding: A toddler's tower falls when she builds alone but stands when her aunt steadies it with one finger, and she celebrates it as entirely her own.

subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
passage: "Dada, stuck!" Sabina held up the fish piece. It would not go into the puzzle board. "Stuck?" said Bhupen, setting down his tea. "Let's see. Try again." She pressed hard. Nothing. "Stuck!" "Hmm. What if the tail goes this way?" He turned the piece a little in her hand. "Now push." Plop. The fish sat in its place. "I did it! Dada, I did it!" "You did," Bhupen said, smiling. "Next one?" "Duck! Me do duck!"

qa.q: Which piece would not go into the puzzle board?
qa.a: The fish piece.

qa.q: What does Sabina's 'I did it! Dada, I did it!' show about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt proud and thrilled, as if the fish went in by her own work alone.

qa.q: What small choice did Bhupen make that helped Sabina succeed?
qa.a: He turned the piece a little in her hand and let her push, so she still did the last step.

qa.q: Why might Bhupen say 'You did' instead of explaining his help?
qa.a: Bhupen wants Sabina to keep her pride and her eagerness to try the next piece.

grounding: A toddler cannot fit a puzzle piece alone, succeeds when her grandfather turns it slightly, and claims the win happily as her own.

subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
passage:
Daycare note, Thursday. Written by Jahnavi.
Rafiq, two, tried to thread the big wooden beads on the lace today. The lace flopped and the bead slid off, four times. He pushed the basket away and whimpered. I held the tip of the lace stiff between two fingers, nothing more. He poked it through, pulled, and the red bead dropped down. He held it up and shouted, "Me did it!" Then he threaded two more alone before snack.

qa.q: How many times did the bead slide off before Rafiq got help?
qa.a: The bead slid off four times.

qa.q: What does Rafiq's shout of 'Me did it!' suggest he feels?
qa.a: He feels proud, as if the win were all his own, even though Jahnavi was holding the lace for him.

qa.q: Which choice of Jahnavi's worked, and why?
qa.a: Holding only the tip of the lace, nothing more, gave Rafiq just enough steadiness to push the bead through himself.

qa.q: What would change for Rafiq if Jahnavi had threaded the bead for him?
qa.a: He would miss the feeling of pulling it through himself, and might not have gone on to thread two more alone.

grounding: A caregiver steadies a lace so a two-year-old can thread a bead he could not manage alone, and he celebrates the win as his own.

subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
passage:
In the potter's courtyard, Sarita, two, wanted to stack the little clay cups like her Nana, Vijay. The third cup always wobbled on the bumpy ground and tumbled into the dust. She scowled at it.
Nana set down his wheel stick and pressed the bottom cup flat with two fingers. Sarita placed the fourth cup. It stayed. The fifth. It stayed. She turned, clapped her dusty hands and shouted, "Sarita did!" Nana laughed and quietly let go.

qa.q: What did Sarita want to stack?
qa.a: She wanted to stack the little clay cups.

qa.q: How can you tell Sarita felt the stack was all her own work?
qa.a: She feels proud and delighted, clapping her dusty hands and shouting 'Sarita did!' as if the stack were all her own work.

qa.q: Why did Nana's small help work better than stacking the cups for her?
qa.a: By only pressing the bottom cup flat, he let her place every cup herself, so the success felt real to her. 🙂

qa.q: What might Vijay Nana be thinking as he laughs and quietly lets go?
qa.a: He is probably pleased and amused, knowing his fingers helped but happy to let her keep the win.

grounding: A grandfather quietly steadies the base so a toddler can stack clay cups she could not manage alone, and she claims the win.
